title: A Inventory for the Interior
premise: After her mother's funeral, Paloma Okafor returns to the family house to inventory its contents and finds a stranger, Adaeze, mourning at the gate—a woman who calls the family by a name no one has spoken in thirty years. As Paloma catalogs rooms full of deliberate omissions, she uncovers evidence that her mother helped a man disappear after a crime he may not have committed, trading her family's silence for his survival. The question the whole household arranged itself around—who was protected, and from what—finally surfaces when Paloma's brother threatens to sell the house and bury the past for good. In the end, Paloma chooses justice outside the law: she gives Adaeze the truth and the documents, accepts estrangement from her brother, and learns that love against duty means letting the family name break open rather than holding it shut.
about_author: Mirabel Eastwick is the pen name of a former estate appraiser who spent a decade cataloging other people's inheritances before writing about her own. She lives near the coast, where she keeps an inventory of things she refuses to throw away.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At the reception after her mother's funeral, Paloma performs flawless grief management, deflecting condolences and her brother Chidi's impatience to sell the house. The emotional beat is controlled numbness—she has inherited her mother's talent for ending conversations with a smile.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Locking up at dusk, she finds a woman waiting at the gate who calls the family by 'Okafordu,' a name Paloma has never heard. The stranger, Adaeze, leaves only a folded paper before vanishing. The beat: the first crack in Paloma's composure.

chapters.title: Inventory of Omissions
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with brief flashbacks in her mother's voice through found letters. Cataloging the house room by room, she notices what's missing: photographs cut apart, a locked desk drawer, a second set of birth records. The beat: unease sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: What the Desk Kept
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She opens the drawer and finds newspaper clippings from 1994—an arson, a dead night watchman, a young man named Emeka Okafordu who was never caught—and letters between her mother and someone signing only 'E.' The beat: vertigo as the family's shape rearranges.

chapters.title: Chidi's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Chidi's POV. Eager to liquidate the estate and escape debt, Chidi discovers Paloma has delayed the sale and confronts her, dismissing the clippings as dangerous sentiment. The beat: sibling fracture; duty versus truth takes sides.

chapters.title: Adaeze, Again
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Paloma and Adaeze. Paloma tracks Adaeze to a laundromat two towns over. Adaeze reveals she is Emeka's daughter and that their mothers were friends until the fire; she has come because her father is dying and wants to confess before it's too late. The beat: reluctant alliance.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV, then Paloma's. Through Adaeze's account and a hidden cassette tape, the truth emerges: Paloma's mother hid Emeka knowing he was innocent of murder but guilty of arson, and let the town believe its own verdict to protect him from a worse one. The beat: grief complicated by admiration.

chapters.title: Time Already Running Out
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Emeka is hospitalized; Chidi, tipped off by a nosy aunt, moves to sell the house within days and destroy the papers as 'clutter.' Paloma must choose between preserving the family's peace and delivering the confession. The beat: rising dread, ticking clock.

chapters.title: The Question the House Was Built Around
chapters.summary: Climax, Paloma's POV. At the hospital, dying Emeka asks Paloma directly whether her mother ever regretted it. Paloma reads him the letters aloud, then publicly gives Adaeze the documents that could reopen the case, defying Chidi in front of the family. The beat: rupture—the smile finally fails.

chapters.title: Everything Accounted For
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, months later. The house sells; Chidi doesn't come to the reading of the will, but sends one uncut photograph. Paloma finishes the inventory, leaving one line blank under her mother's name, and visits Adaeze and recovering Emeka. The beat: quiet resolution—justice without absolution, love without the old duty.
